erratum_note: No erratum appended: every rechecked claim class returned supported or, for [P50], supported at the catalogue level the entry itself declares. Nothing in the entry needed correction on the evidence retrieved, and no deleted flags or rewritten scholarship was contemplated.
assigned_scope: 02 CONNECTOR (read-only) + SOURCE-RECHECK for the language/myth/material/era entry; report at reports/supplement-opencode-1/02-interface-map.md

coupling_audits: A1/A2 name-to-piety coupling (naming practices vs myth/era: theophoric names against a Ramesside-only boundary)
A3 material-to-era coupling (a dated Amarna dress fragment used as representation evidence)
A4 era-to-calendar coupling (civil/religious track separation and the refused festival-date equation)

audits.claim: The entry says [SZ03] invokes theophoric names against restricting personal piety to the Ramesside age (line 92, naming practices row; line 96 restates it).
audits.source_locator: Review of Assmann, The Search for God in Ancient Egypt, by Kasia Szpakowska, Electronic Antiquity 7(1), unpaginated HTML; paragraph beginning 'There are also problems in attributing personal piety to the Ramesside age alone' (no page numbers are printed in the HTML review)
audits.source_excerpt: Personal piety may have found other means of expression in earlier time periods, such as theophoric names, scarab formulae, and even in early Eighteenth Dynasty prayers.
audits.basis: The retrieved review sentence is the source of the entry's claim, at the level of argument (a named scholarly challenge), not a world-fact. The entry's own framing ('Szpakowska invokes them against restricting personal piety to the Ramesside age') matches the retrieved text and does not overstate it.
audits.access_limit: None for this source: full review text retrieved from the journal's institutional host (Virginia Tech Scholarly Communication). The review itself is unpaginated in HTML, so no page-level locator is offered.

audits.claim: The entry says [SZ03] documents non-Atenist amulets/figurines at Amarna that complicate universal replacement (line 88, mythic/pantheon core row; line 182 limits household evidence).
audits.source_locator: same review, paragraph beginning 'He describes how uncomfortable life was for the common man' (sentence after the single-hymn criticism)
audits.source_excerpt: in the workman's village of Amarna itself, excavations have revealed the presence of non-Atenist amulets and figurines attesting to at least the continued worship of household deities.
audits.basis: Retrieved sentence supports the entry's evidence claim and its caution ('do not infer a complete clandestine belief system from one object'): the review itself hedges with 'at least the continued worship'.
audits.access_limit: Same as A1; the sentence's underlying excavation reports were not inspected, and the audit is review-level evidence only.

audits.claim: The entry says [M531] is a limestone fragment catalogued as New Kingdom, Amarna Period, reign of Akhenaten, ca. 1347–1330 BCE, depicting a pleated dress, used for depiction evidence only (lines 12, 91).
audits.source_locator: Met Collection API object record, objectID 550026, accessionNumber 21.9.531, fields period/reign/objectDate/medium/title/subregion; metadataDate 2026-07-31T04:50:42.63Z
audits.source_excerpt: "period": "New Kingdom, Amarna Period", "dynasty": "Dynasty 18", "reign": "reign of Akhenaten", "objectDate": "ca. 1347–1330 BCE", "title": "Side of body in pleated dress"
audits.basis: Every catalogue field the entry quotes matches the retrieved record, and the record's medium ("Siliceous indurated limestone", dimensions H. 11 x W. 5 x D. 2 cm) supports the entry's insistence that this is representation evidence for depicted pleating, not a recovered garment. The record also confirms the elite/temple context the entry flags as source bias (subregion 'Amarna (Akhetaten)', locale 'Great Temple of the Aten', Petrie/Carter 1891-92).
audits.access_limit: The human-facing page https://www.metmuseum.org/art/collection/search/550026 returned HTTP 429 to this environment; the official collection API JSON was retrieved instead (exit 0). The machine-readable date range (objectBeginDate -1353, objectEndDate -1336) is wider than the displayed catalogue string the entry quotes; the entry quotes the displayed attribution, and its own caveat ('the object's current catalogue attribution, not a universal reign chronology') remains correct.

audits.claim: The entry says [P50] is a foundational reconstruction of a civil calendar alongside lunar religious calendars, that its origins proposal requires calibration, and that the entry asserts no Amarna festival-to-civil-date equation (lines 11, 32, 93, 181).
audits.source_locator: ISAC institutional publication record for Parker, The Calendars of Ancient Egypt (SAOC 26), description paragraph
audits.source_excerpt: Parker demonstrates that the Egyptians had three calendars, two lunar and religious, one civil.
audits.basis: The institutional record supports the entry's structural claim and, in the following sentences ('suggests a possible origin for the civil calendar', excursus solutions), supports its reconstruction-level calibration of Parker. The entry asserts no specific festival equation, and nothing retrieved contradicts that restraint; the audit therefore cannot and does not verify any such equation.
audits.access_limit: Catalogue-level record only, exactly as the entry states ('[P50] was inspected at catalogue level only'); the book's own text and calendar tables were not retrieved. Unresolved festival-date questions remain unresolved.

audits.claim: The entry says Egyptian is a distinct branch of Afroasiatic and that Allen uses the older label 'Hamito-Semitic' while 'Hamitic' is not a valid racial population category (line 86).
audits.source_locator: Allen, The Ancient Egyptian Language (CUP 2013), publisher excerpt PDF, 10 pages, §§1.1-1.2; the 'distinct branch' sentence is on excerpt page 2 (printed page 2), paragraph after the Hamito-Semitic feature list
audits.source_excerpt: These peculiarities identify Egyptian as a distinct branch within the Hamito-Semitic language family, with no close relatives of its own
audits.basis: Retrieved verbatim from the entry's own cited source (downloaded, pdftotext, 452 lines). The same excerpt uses 'Hamito-Semitic' throughout (5 occurrences; 0 for 'Afroasiatic'), which is exactly the label caution the entry records. The entry's warning against 'Hamitic' as a racial category is its own calibration statement, not attributed to Allen, and nothing retrieved contradicts it.
audits.access_limit: Publisher excerpt only (10 pages of a monograph); §1.1-1.2 retrieved, not the whole book. The PDF had to be downloaded and converted locally (pdftotext); the FetchURL tool could not extract it.

audits.claim: The entry's language staging row: Late Egyptian appears in writing around Akhenaten and becomes standard in the following dynasty, and a written debut is not the birth of a spoken language (line 87).
audits.source_locator: Allen 2013 excerpt PDF, §1.2 'Historical overview', sentence on excerpt page 3 (printed page 3), immediately after the traditional Middle Egyptian sentence
audits.source_excerpt: Late Egyptian began to appear in texts from the time of Akhenaten (Dynasty XVIII, c. 1350 bc) and became the standard written language in the succeeding dynasty.
audits.basis: The entry's staging sentence is a faithful paraphrase of the retrieved source sentence, and the source itself separates written debut from spoken change ('By the time the latter appeared in writing, Middle Egyptian had ceased to be a living language'), supporting the entry's 'a written debut is not the birth of a spoken language' caution. Corroborating classification: Glottolog 5.3 lists 'Late Egyptian' as a stage under Egyptian {Ancient} (languoid late1256, classification Afro-Asiatic > Egyptian > Egyptian (Ancient)).
audits.access_limit: Excerpt-level retrieval of the cited book; the two-stage Egypt I/Egypt II grouping was read in the excerpt but its chapters were not.

audits.claim: The entry's language-family column rests on Egyptian belonging to Afroasiatic as a family designation (line 184: 'Afroasiatic is a language-family designation, not an ethnic essence').
audits.source_locator: Glottolog 5.3 languoid record egyp1245 'Egyptian' (family, level=family), fields classification/child_language_count/newick; cross-checked record late1256 'Late Egyptian'
audits.basis: Glottolog classifies 'Egyptian' directly under Afro-Asiatic (a family under family afro1255) with no intermediate node, matching 'distinct branch'; its stammbaum separates the stages Old/Middle/Late Egyptian, Demotic, Coptic under Egyptian {Ancient}. This is classification-level evidence for the family designation and does not bear on the entry's warning against ethnic readings.
audits.access_limit: Glottolog's HTML page for the languoid extracted only its header, so the machine-readable JSON records were retrieved instead (curl, exit 0). Glottolog is a classification catalogue; it does not date the stages.
